screens.title: Dynamic Memory Allocation with new and delete
screens.subtitle: How to allocate and free heap memory safely in C++

narration.text: In this chapter you'll learn how C++ lets you request memory at runtime and why that control is essential. Heap allocation with the new family of operators allows programs to create objects whose size or lifetime is not known at compile time — for example, reading an unknown number of entries from a file or building data structures that grow and shrink. You'll see the exact syntax for allocating a single object and for allocating arrays, and you will practice the matching deallocation rules that prevent memory leaks and corruptions. We'll walk through concrete examples: allocating a single integer, allocating an array of doubles, and returning a dynamically allocated list of strings from a function. You'll also learn the common mistakes to avoid: failing to delete memory, using the wrong delete form for arrays, double frees, and leaving dangling pointers. Finally, we'll connect these manual techniques to the reason we later prefer RAII and smart pointers: exception safety and predictable cleanup. As you move through the lesson, think about when you would choose dynamic allocation and what ownership model you will use to make your code robust.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Use new/new[] to request heap memory and always match with delete/delete[] to avoid leaks and undefined behavior.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives give you practical, verifiable skills. First, you'll allocate single objects and arrays on the heap using new and new[] so you can create data whose size or lifetime is only known at runtime. You'll practice assigning values and using pointers to access heap-allocated memory. Second, you'll deallocate those objects correctly with delete and delete[] so that memory is returned to the system and destructors run for each element where appropriate. Third, you'll learn to match allocation and deallocation forms — using delete for single objects and delete[] for arrays — because mismatching them is undefined behavior and a source of crashes. Finally, you'll begin to handle error cases such as null pointers and learn patterns that avoid memory leaks. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual to solidify the concept and a verified competency milestone so you can confirm mastery by writing small programs that allocate, use, and free memory safely.

screens.title: The new operator: allocate a single object
screens.subtitle: How new requests heap memory and returns a pointer

narration.text: Let's define the new operator and what it does in practice. When you write new followed by a type, the runtime allocates enough memory on the heap for one object of that type, constructs it, and returns a pointer to its first byte. This pointer is an address you can store in a raw pointer variable and use to read or write the object. A concrete example is allocating an integer: you request a single int on the heap, assign a value through the pointer, and then read it back. A common misconception is that heap memory is magically managed; it is not. If you allocate with new and never delete, the memory remains reserved until the program ends. Another subtle point is that new typically throws std::bad_alloc on failure, so production code may need to handle exceptions or use nothrow forms. Practical tip: after you delete a pointer, set it to nullptr so future checks can safely determine whether the pointer is valid. Reflect: when would you prefer heap allocation over automatic stack variables in a small program, and who owns that memory?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: new constructs an object on the heap and returns a pointer; you are responsible for freeing it.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › The new operator
Core Concept
What new does
Allocates memory, constructs the object, returns a pointer to it. You own it until you delete it.
Key bullets
  • new allocates and constructs a single object on the heap and returns a pointer.
  • If allocation fails, new typically throws std::bad_alloc.
  • You must delete the returned pointer to free memory and call the destructor.
  • After delete set pointer to nullptr to prevent dangling pointers.
Example
Allocate an int on the heap, assign 100, then delete it and set the pointer to nullptr.
Key Takeaway

Use new for heap lifetime control, but always plan who deletes the memory.

Code example
int* myIntPtr = new int; // Allocates one integer on the heap
*myIntPtr = 100;         // Assign via pointer
std::cout << *myIntPtr << std::endl;

// When finished:
delete myIntPtr;         // Free the heap memory
myIntPtr = nullptr;      // Prevent dangling pointer
Common mistake
Forgetting delete causes a memory leak; relying on program end to free memory is unsafe for long-running processes.
Pro tip
Consider ownership: mark who must delete the pointer and set it to nullptr immediately after deletion.

screens.title: Allocating arrays with new[]
screens.subtitle: Syntax, element access, and initialization behavior

narration.text: Allocating an array on the heap uses new followed by type and square brackets with a size. This creates a contiguous block of memory large enough to hold the requested number of elements and returns a pointer to the first element. For built-in types like double or int, default initialization depends on whether you use value-initialization; plain new double[N] leaves built-in types uninitialized, while default-constructed classes call their default constructor for each element. A concrete example from the chapter allocates five doubles and fills them in a loop. A common misconception is that arrays allocated with new[] behave exactly like std::vector; they do not. You must manage size, bounds, and lifetime manually. When indexing, you use usual array syntax on the returned pointer. Finally, remember that arrays must be deallocated with delete[], not delete. Ask yourself: when should you use a raw new[] array rather than a standard container, and how will you ensure ownership is clear? Allocating arrays with new[] means new[] allocates a block for many objects; you must track size and free with delete[].. In practical terms, syntax, element access, and initialization behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Array allocation
keyIdea.text: new[] allocates a block for many objects; you must track size and free with delete[].

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › new[] Arrays
Process
Allocate and use an array
Create a contiguous block, assign elements by index, and manage size and lifetime manually.
  • new Type[count] returns a pointer to the first element.
  • Built-in types may be uninitialized unless value-initialized.
  • Keep track of the array length; there is no built-in size metadata.
  • Always free with delete[] to invoke all destructors and return the whole block.
Key Takeaway
Use new[] for simple manual arrays but prefer containers when you need automatic size and lifetime management.
Code example
int arraySize = 5;
double* myDoubleArray = new double[arraySize]; // allocate 5 doubles
for (int i = 0; i < arraySize; ++i) {
  myDoubleArray[i] = static_cast<double>(i) * 1.5;
}
// use elements...
// Correct deallocation:
delete[] myDoubleArray;
myDoubleArray = nullptr;
Common misconception
Treating raw arrays like vectors ignores size, capacity, and exception safety; prefer std::vector for most use cases.

screens.title: delete vs delete[] — why matching matters
screens.subtitle: How mismatches cause undefined behavior

narration.text: A central safety rule is to match how memory was allocated with how you free it. If you allocate a single object with new, you must use delete. If you allocate an array with new[], you must use delete[]. Using delete on memory allocated with new[] is undefined behavior: destructors for all elements might not be called and the memory block may not be properly returned to the heap, leading to corruption or crashes. Conversely, delete[] on memory allocated with new is also incorrect. A concrete contrast: deleting a five-element array with plain delete may only call the first element's destructor, leaving the rest unreclaimed. A common misconception is that delete and delete[] are interchangeable because both appear to free memory; they are not. Key practice: record allocation form in your ownership conventions and, whenever possible, encapsulate allocation and deallocation in a single owner so mismatches cannot occur. Think of it as matching brackets — the syntax and semantics must pair. delete vs delete[] — why matching matters means always use delete for new and delete[] for new[]; mixing them causes undefined behavior.. In practical terms, how mismatches cause undefined behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Match forms
keyIdea.text: Always use delete for new and delete[] for new[]; mixing them causes undefined behavior.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › delete vs delete[]
Comparison
Single object (new) vs Array (new[])
Which deallocator to use changes how destructors are run and how memory is released.
Allocated with new
Use delete. delete[] is incorrect and may try to read deallocation metadata that isn't present.
Allocated with new[]
Use delete[]. delete may call only first destructor and fail to free whole block.
Common mistake
Assuming delete is 'good enough' for arrays. This leads to subtle runtime corruption.
Illustrative scenario
Imagine default-constructed objects in an array have non-trivial destructors. If delete[] is not used, some destructors won't run and resources referenced by those objects won't be released, causing leaks and potential resource corruption.
Check your understanding

Which deallocation is correct for MyObject* a = new MyObject[10]; ?

Answer: delete[] a; because the allocation used new[].
Key Takeaway

Treat allocation and deallocation forms as a pair; mismatches are undefined behavior.

screens.title: Safe deallocation: delete pattern
screens.subtitle: Delete, set to nullptr, and avoid double free

narration.text: Deallocating memory safely is a small sequence of disciplined steps. First, ensure that the pointer still owns the memory and has not been transferred or already freed. Second, call the correct form of delete. Third, immediately set the pointer to nullptr. This prevents accidental double frees and makes future null checks safe. A concrete example is allocating a pointer, using it, deleting it, and then setting it to nullptr. A frequent mistake is attempting to delete the same pointer twice — this can corrupt the heap and produce undefined behavior. Another trap is leaving a pointer with the address of freed memory; dereferencing it will likely crash the program. Finally, in complex functions with multiple exit points or exceptions, ensure every early return or thrown exception cannot bypass deallocation. If you find that pattern repeated, encapsulate it in an owner object so only the owner deletes in its destructor. Ask: who is responsible for deletion in your functions? Safe deallocation: delete pattern means delete the owned memory, then set the pointer to nullptr to prevent double deletes and dangling dereferences.. In practical terms, delete, set to nullptr, and avoid double free. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Delete pattern
keyIdea.text: Delete the owned memory, then set the pointer to nullptr to prevent double deletes and dangling dereferences.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Safe deallocation
Process Flow
Steps for safe deletion
  1. Confirm ownership and that the pointer is not nullptr.
  2. Call delete or delete[] as appropriate.
  3. Set the pointer to nullptr immediately after delete.
  4. Avoid using the pointer after deletion; check for nullptr before dereferencing.
Example pattern
delete ptr; ptr = nullptr; — simple but powerful to avoid double free and dangling pointer errors.
Common mistakes & checks
  • Double free: calling delete twice on the same memory corrupts the heap.
  • Dangling pointer: pointer still points to freed memory; dereferencing causes undefined behavior.
  • Null deletion is safe: delete nullptr; does nothing, so setting pointer to nullptr is a defensive practice.
Check your understanding
True or False: Setting ptr = nullptr replaces the need to call delete. (Answer: False — nullptr prevents dangling dereference but does not free memory unless delete was called beforehand.)

screens.title: std::bad_alloc and allocation failure
screens.subtitle: What happens when new cannot allocate memory

narration.text: When a request with new cannot be fulfilled because the system lacks the required free memory, the usual behavior is for new to throw a std::bad_alloc exception. That means your allocation call will not return a pointer; instead, control flow jumps to the nearest handler. A concrete consequence is that if you allocate memory and then later in the same function allocate another resource, an exception thrown before you delete the first allocation can cause a leak. This is an important reason to write exception-safe code: if you don't free memory on every path out of a function, you leak. A common misconception is that new returns a null pointer on failure; modern C++ throws instead. There is a nothrow overload that returns nullptr, but relying on it changes semantics and still requires careful cleanup. The safer long-term technique is RAII: wrap resources in objects whose destructors run during stack unwinding so memory is released automatically. Reflect: how would you structure a function that allocates two resources to avoid leaks when the second allocation fails? std::bad_alloc and allocation failure means new throws std::bad_alloc on failure; plan cleanup paths or use raii to ensure no leaks during exceptions.. In practical terms, what happens when new cannot allocate memory. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Allocation failure
keyIdea.text: new throws std::bad_alloc on failure; plan cleanup paths or use RAII to ensure no leaks during exceptions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › std::bad_alloc
Definition
When allocation fails
new throws an exception on allocation failure. Handle it or use RAII to avoid leaks during unwinding.
  • Default new throws std::bad_alloc; nothrow variant returns nullptr.
  • If an exception occurs after an allocation and you did not free, a leak can happen.
  • Encapsulating resources in objects ensures destructors run during stack unwinding.
Scenario
Allocate A with new, then allocate B. If B fails and throws, A must be freed or wrapped so it is cleaned automatically. This is the heart of exception-safety concerns and the motivation for RAII.
Misconception check
Incorrect: assuming new returns nullptr on failure in modern C++. Correct: handle std::bad_alloc or use nothrow form and check for nullptr.
Key Takeaway

Design allocation so that resources are either freed in every path or owned by RAII objects that free themselves.

screens.title: Returning a dynamically allocated array from a function
screens.subtitle: createStudentNames: ownership and lifetime

narration.text: The chapter example shows a function that returns a pointer to a dynamically allocated array of strings. This pattern is educational but carries clear ownership questions: who is responsible for delete[]? In the example, the caller receives ownership and must call delete[] when finished. The function also returns nullptr for invalid counts, which the caller must check. This example highlights two practical points: always document ownership transfer and check for nullptr before dereferencing returned pointers. A misconception to avoid is assuming returned pointers are always valid; you must check against nullptr if the function uses that signal. Concrete walkthrough: the function allocates an array of strings, fills each entry with a generated name, and returns the pointer. The caller then prints entries and calls delete[] followed by setting the pointer to nullptr. Ask yourself: how could you redesign this function using a container or RAII so the caller does not need to manage deletion manually? Returning a dynamically allocated array from a function means if a function returns a raw pointer to heap memory, the caller typically owns and must delete[] it; document and check for nullptr.. In practical terms, createstudentnames: ownership and lifetime. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Ownership rule
keyIdea.text: If a function returns a raw pointer to heap memory, the caller typically owns and must delete[] it; document and check for nullptr.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › createStudentNames
Code Walkthrough
Function allocates an array of std::string, fills each element, and returns the pointer. Caller checks for nullptr, uses the array, then delete[] and sets to nullptr.
std::string* createStudentNames(int count) {
  if (count <= 0) return nullptr;
  std::string* names = new std::string[count];
  for (int i = 0; i < count; ++i) {
    names[i] = "Student_" + std::to_string(i + 1);
  }
  return names; // Caller owns and must delete[]
}

// Caller:
int numStudents = 3;
std::string* studentList = createStudentNames(numStudents);
if (studentList != nullptr) {
  // use studentList
  delete[] studentList;
  studentList = nullptr;
}
Notes and pitfalls
  • Document that the function transfers ownership to the caller.
  • Caller must delete[] to free all elements and avoid leaks.
  • Consider returning a standard container to avoid manual ownership semantics.
Key Takeaway
Raw returned pointers make ownership explicit but error-prone; prefer RAII when possible.

screens.title: Product class lab: allocate and deallocate an array of objects
screens.subtitle: Constructors, destructors, and delete[] behavior

narration.text: The hands-on activity in the chapter uses a Product class to show object lifecycle on the heap. When you call new Product[numProducts], the default constructor runs for each array element. Later, when you assign a product into an array slot, the temporary product is copy-assigned to the element. At the end, delete[] products calls the destructor for every element, demonstrating how allocation and deallocation of objects differ from plain data types. A common misconception is that delete[] only frees memory and does not run destructors — it does run destructors for each element in the array. The activity also shows what happens if you comment out delete[]: destructors are not called and resources held by those objects may never be released. As you run the exercise, watch the console output that prints constructor and destructor messages; this is a vivid way to see object lifetime. Question to reflect on: how would ownership and cleanup change if exceptions occurred during population of the array? Product class lab: allocate and deallocate an array of objects means new[] calls constructors for each element; delete[] calls destructors for each element — essential for object lifetime correctness.. In practical terms, constructors, destructors, and delete[] behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Object arrays
keyIdea.text: new[] calls constructors for each element; delete[] calls destructors for each element — essential for object lifetime correctness.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Product lab
Activity
Allocate an array of Products
Observe constructor and destructor calls and practice correct delete[] usage.
Product* products = nullptr;
try {
  products = new Product[numProducts];
} catch (const std::bad_alloc& e) {
  // handle failure
}
// populate products[i] = Product(name, price);
// later:
delete[] products;
products = nullptr;
Observations
  • new Product[n] calls default constructor n times.
  • Assigning into elements can create temporaries and use copy assignment.
  • delete[] calls all destructors; without it, destructors won't run.
Common pitfall
If population code throws an exception, ensure allocated array is still freed — this is why RAII is recommended.

screens.title: Memory leak demonstration and fix
screens.subtitle: Intentional leak example and the corrected code

narration.text: The chapter gives a clear intentional leak example: allocating memory in a loop without calling delete. This demonstrates how memory usage grows over repeated allocations and why leaks matter in long-running programs. The leaked pointer goes out of scope, leaving the heap memory unreachable and reserved. The fix is straightforward: after using allocated memory, call delete or delete[] as appropriate and set the pointer to nullptr. The chapter shows a fix where the function deallocates the memory before returning. A misconception to watch for is thinking that letting the pointer go out of scope frees memory automatically; it does not. Practice: run the leaking loop a few times and observe memory growth, then apply the fix and observe stable memory. Finally, consider how RAII would have prevented the leak by tying allocation to an object's destructor, so cleanup happens even if a function returns early or throws. Memory leak demonstration and fix means a memory leak happens when allocated memory is never freed; always call delete/delete[] on every allocation path or use raii to automate cleanup.. In practical terms, intentional leak example and the corrected code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Leak vs fix
keyIdea.text: A memory leak happens when allocated memory is never freed; always call delete/delete[] on every allocation path or use RAII to automate cleanup.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Memory leak demo
Leaking example
A loop allocates ints and never deletes them, causing memory consumption to grow.
void createLeak() {
  int* data = new int[100];
  // ... use data ...
  // forgot delete[] data; -> leak
}
Fixed version
Call delete[] before letting the pointer go out of scope, and set pointer to nullptr.
void fixLeak() {
  int* data = new int[100];
  // ... use data ...
  delete[] data; // free memory
  data = nullptr;
}
Key Takeaway
Always free every allocation on every path, or use RAII wrappers that free automatically.

screens.title: Why RAII and smart pointers matter
screens.subtitle: Exception safety and automated cleanup

narration.text: Manual new and delete give you fine-grained control but also introduce risk. A primary motivation for RAII is exception safety: when objects own resources and their destructors free them, stack unwinding during exceptions automatically runs cleanup code. Smart pointers like unique_ptr and shared_ptr implement RAII for heap-allocated objects, preventing most leaks and double frees by giving ownership semantics to pointer-like objects. The chapter briefly introduces RAII as the next step after raw allocation. A concrete contrast: in code that allocates two resources, if the second allocation throws, RAII ensures the first resource's destructor runs; with raw pointers it may not. A misconception is that RAII removes the need to understand raw allocation; in fact, understanding new and delete helps you use RAII correctly and decide when ownership transfer is appropriate. Reflect: how would you convert a raw pointer return to a function into a return of a smart pointer to improve safety? Why RAII and smart pointers matter means raii ties resource lifetime to object lifetime so destructors run on all paths, solving many manual allocation pitfalls.. In practical terms, exception safety and automated cleanup. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: RAII motivation
keyIdea.text: RAII ties resource lifetime to object lifetime so destructors run on all paths, solving many manual allocation pitfalls.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › RAII and Smart Pointers
Architecture
Ownership model: manual vs RAII
Wrap heap resources in objects whose destructor frees them. This makes all exit paths safe.
Manual: raw pointer returned, caller must delete.
RAII: return an owning object so destructor frees memory automatically.
Why this matters
RAII reduces human error around multiple exit paths and exceptions. It also clarifies ownership: one owner is responsible for cleanup and transfer semantics are explicit with smart pointers.
Key Takeaway
Prefer RAII to manage heap resources; use raw new/delete only when you clearly document ownership and cleanup paths.

screens.title: Finding and fixing memory errors
screens.subtitle: Practical checks: nullptr, destructor messages, and running leak scenarios

narration.text: When debugging memory problems, use small, reproducible tests. For leaks, run a tight loop that allocates memory and monitor memory usage; the chapter suggests observing a task manager to see growth. For object lifetime, add logging in constructors and destructors to confirm which destructors run and which do not. Always check pointers for nullptr before dereferencing if a function may return null. A useful practice is to write tests that allocate and free in every code path, including error and exception paths. A common misconception is that occasional leaks are harmless — small leaks can accumulate in long-running processes and lead to failures. Another practical tip is to set pointers to nullptr after deletion and to avoid raw pointer aliasing across ownership boundaries. Reflect: when you inspect constructor and destructor messages for an array, do you see N constructor calls and N destructor calls? If not, inspect allocation and deallocation forms. Finding and fixing memory errors means reproduce leaks in a loop, log constructors/destructors, and ensure every allocation has a matching deallocation on all paths.. In practical terms, practical checks: nullptr, destructor messages, and running leak scenarios. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Debug tips
keyIdea.text: Reproduce leaks in a loop, log constructors/destructors, and ensure every allocation has a matching deallocation on all paths.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Debugging memory
Process
Reproduce, observe, fix
  • Reproduce a leak with a short loop that repeatedly allocates without freeing.
  • Instrument constructors/destructors to see lifecycle events in the console.
  • Check for mismatched delete/delete[] and for missing delete calls on early returns.
Practical checks
If destructors are not called for array elements, check whether delete[] was used. If memory usage grows, identify leaked allocations and ensure delete executes on every code path. Setting pointers to nullptr after delete makes checks safer and avoids accidental reuse.
Reflection
When logging shows fewer destructor calls than constructor calls, you likely have a mismatched or missing delete.

screens.title: Assessment ideas and quiz review
screens.subtitle: Check understanding with targeted questions and code fixes

narration.text: Assessments should test pairing rules, leak recognition, and safe cleanup. narration.text: Let's summarize the essential concepts to carry forward. First, the new operator allocates memory on the heap and returns a pointer; you must manage that memory's lifetime. Second, delete frees a single object and delete[] frees arrays — matching is mandatory to avoid undefined behavior. Third, memory leaks occur when allocated memory becomes unreachable because it was not freed; small leaks can accumulate in long-running programs. These three ideas form the backbone of safe manual memory management. Keep these rules in mind as you practice the lab and prepare to adopt RAII in later chapters for more robust, exception-safe code. Summary takeaway: Manual heap management gives control but requires strict ownership discipline. Use nullptr assignments, match new/delete forms, and prefer RAII to avoid common failures.

narration.text: A few final definitions to keep handy. Double free is when the same memory block is deleted more than once; it corrupts the heap and causes undefined behavior. A dangling pointer points at memory that has already been freed; dereferencing it is dangerous. std::bad_alloc signals allocation failure; handle it or design code so destructors free prior allocations. These definitions highlight the errors you want to prevent as you practice manual allocation. When you see these problems in your programs, step back and ask which object owns each allocation and how lifetime will be enforced. That's the core thinking that prevents bugs.
